text: Setting up the AI service locally starts with a virtual environment. From the ai-service folder in PowerShell, run python -m venv .venv to create the environment, activate it with .\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1, and then install the declared dependencies using pip install -r requirements.txt. Python 3.10 or newer must already be present on the PATH before any of this works. Keeping the environment inside the service folder rather than at the repository root means each service owns its own dependency set and nothing leaks between them.

The FastAPI application is served by uvicorn. With the virtual environment still activated and the shell still inside the ai-service folder, run uvicorn app.main:app --reload --port 8000. That window stays occupied for as long as the server runs, so any further commands need a second terminal. The --reload flag watches the source tree and restarts the process whenever a file changes, which is convenient during development but should never be used when the service is deployed for real traffic.

To confirm the service is alive, send a request to the placeholder query endpoint from a second terminal: Invoke-RestMethod -Uri http://localhost:8000/query -Method Post -ContentType application/json -Body '{"query":"test"}'. The same call can be made from Bruno by choosing POST, entering the URL, and supplying a JSON body. The response echoes the submitted query, returns a fixed placeholder answer explaining that the retrieval pipeline is not implemented, and includes an empty sources array.

Before touching any schema, confirm that the database engine is actually running. On Windows the PowerShell command Get-Service -Name postgresql* lists every installed Postgres service along with its current state. If the service shows as stopped, start it from the Services application or with Start-Service. A stopped engine produces connection-refused errors that are easy to mistake for credential problems, so this check is worth doing first whenever connections fail unexpectedly.

The gateway configuration expects a login role and a database that are both named genrag, with genrag as the default password, all three overridable through environment variables. In pgAdmin, connect to the server, right-click Login/Group Roles and create a role named genrag with a password and the can-login flag enabled. Then right-click Databases, create a database named genrag, and set its owner to the role just created. Getting the ownership right avoids permission errors later when tables are created.

The core relational tables covering users, chats, messages and documents are created by a plain SQL script that lives under the gateway source tree. Select the target database in the pgAdmin tree, open the Query Tool from the Tools menu, load the schema file, and execute it with F5. Afterwards, refresh the Tables node under Schemas and public to confirm that all four tables appear. There is no migration framework wired up on either side of the system yet, so every schema change is applied by hand.

The vector extension is not bundled with the database distribution and is not offered through Stack Builder for the current major version on Windows, so it has to be compiled from source. Install the C++ desktop development workload through the Visual Studio Installer, then open the x64 Native Tools Command Prompt, which is required because it preloads the compiler environment. Clone the extension repository at a recent release tag, point the root variable at the database installation directory, and run the Windows makefile twice, once to build and once to install.

Pick the extension release tag carefully. Version 0.8.0 fails to compile against the newest database major release because the signature of an internal vacuum delay function changed upstream. Version 0.8.5 was current at the time of writing and additionally carries a security fix first shipped in 0.8.2. If the install step fails with a permissions error, close the terminal, reopen the native tools command prompt as an administrator, and re-run the build and install commands from the cloned directory.

After the extension binaries are installed the database engine must be restarted before it will notice them. Open the Services application through services.msc, locate the Postgres service entry, and restart it. Then open the Query Tool against the application database and run CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector. If that statement succeeds the extension is correctly installed and the vector column type becomes available. If it reports that the extension is not available, the build output landed in the wrong installation directory.

The chunk table is created by a second SQL script owned by the AI service rather than the gateway. It must be executed after the base tables exist, because it declares a foreign key that references the documents table. Running it creates the chunk table together with an approximate nearest neighbour index. Verify by refreshing the Tables node, confirming the new table is listed, and expanding its Indexes node to check that the vector index was created alongside it.

Each row in the chunk table carries an identity primary key, a document reference, a chunk index, the chunk text, the embedding vector, and a creation timestamp. The document reference cascades on delete, so removing a document automatically removes every chunk derived from it. A uniqueness constraint spanning the document reference and the chunk index prevents the same ordinal position being inserted twice for one document, which is the failure mode you get when an ingestion job is retried without first clearing partial results.

The embedding column is declared with a fixed width of 768 values, but that number is explicitly marked in the script as a placeholder chosen before any model was selected. The declared width must match the output width of whichever model is finally adopted; a mismatch is rejected at insert time rather than silently truncated. Because the width is part of the column type, changing it later is a schema migration that also invalidates every vector already stored, since vectors produced by different models are not comparable.

The similarity index is an inverted-file flat index built over the embedding column using the cosine distance operator class, configured with one hundred lists. The comment in the script notes that the list count should be revisited once chunking behaviour is settled. This index type partitions vectors into clusters and searches only the nearest few at query time, which trades a small amount of recall for a large reduction in comparisons. It must be built after data is loaded, because empty tables produce degenerate clusters.

The users table keys on a generated UUID and stores a username and an email address, both constrained to be unique, alongside a hashed password and creation and update timestamps. Uniqueness is enforced at the database level rather than only in application code, so a race between two concurrent registration requests for the same address fails cleanly on the constraint instead of producing duplicate accounts. Every other table in the schema ultimately references this one.

Chats belong to a user and carry a title plus creation and update timestamps, indexed by owner and descending update time so that a user's most recent conversations can be listed without a sort. Messages belong to a chat, carry a role constrained to user, assistant or system, hold their text content, and are indexed by chat and ascending creation time so a conversation replays in order. Both tables cascade on delete from their parent.

The documents table records the owning user, the original file name, the storage path, the declared content type, the size in bytes, and a lifecycle status constrained to one of processing, uploaded, indexed or failed. It is indexed by owner so that listing a user's uploads is cheap. The status column is the hook intended for asynchronous ingestion: a freshly stored file is uploaded, a running ingestion job marks it processing, and the terminal states record whether embedding succeeded.

The upload path rejects an empty submission, checks the declared content type against the allowed list, and enforces a maximum size before any storage happens. Only after those checks does it resolve the owning user, persist a metadata row, derive the file extension, and hand the bytes to the storage layer. The metadata row is written before the file is stored, which means a storage failure can leave a database row with no corresponding file on disk unless the surrounding transaction rolls it back.

The storage layer decides which uploads are acceptable by comparing the declared MIME type against exactly two values: portable document format and plain text. Anything else is refused. Because the check reads the content type supplied by the client rather than inspecting the bytes, a mislabelled file passes validation, so the parsing stage downstream cannot assume the declared type is truthful. Widening the set of accepted formats is a change to this method, not merely a change to whatever component extracts text.

Files are written to a configured directory on the local filesystem, named by the generated document identifier plus the original extension rather than by the original file name. Parent directories are created on demand. Naming by identifier avoids collisions between two users uploading files with the same name and removes any path-traversal risk carried by user-supplied names. Retrieval resolves the same identifier and extension back to a path and returns it as a readable resource, failing loudly if the file is missing or unreadable.

Authentication issues a pair of tokens, a short-lived access token and a longer-lived refresh token, each signed with its own configured secret and each carrying its own configured lifetime. The defaults are one day for access and thirty days for refresh, and every one of those values is supplied through environment variables with a development fallback baked into the properties file. Shipping a real deployment with the fallback secrets in place would let anyone forge a valid token.

A servlet filter runs ahead of the controllers, extracts the bearer token from the incoming request, validates its signature and expiry, and populates the security context with the authenticated user identifier. Controllers then receive that identifier directly as an injected authentication principal rather than parsing it themselves, which keeps token handling in exactly one place. Requests that carry no token, or a token that fails validation, never reach the controller layer at all.

When a conversation is loaded by identifier, the service checks that the record actually belongs to the requesting user and reports a chat owned by somebody else exactly the same way it reports one that does not exist. Returning an identical error for both cases matters: distinguishing them would let a caller probe identifiers and learn which conversations exist without having any access to them. The same pattern is applied on both the read path and the send path.

The call from the gateway into the AI service is written so that it never throws. If the downstream service is unreachable, returns a non-success status, or returns a body with no answer field, the method logs the problem and returns a fixed apology string, which the caller then stores as an ordinary assistant message. The effect is that a broken retrieval backend degrades the conversation instead of failing the request outright, and the user sees a reply rather than an error page.

Sending a message runs inside a single database transaction that saves the user message, calls the downstream service over HTTP, and then saves the assistant reply. Because the network call sits inside the transaction, the database connection stays checked out of the pool for the entire duration of the remote call. The configuration comments acknowledge this directly and bound the exposure with an explicit connect timeout of three seconds and a read timeout of sixty seconds rather than leaving either unbounded.

The HTTP client used to reach the downstream service is configured with separate connect and read timeouts, defaulting to three seconds and sixty seconds respectively and both overridable by environment variable. The connect timeout bounds how long the caller waits to establish a socket, which should be fast on a healthy network; the read timeout bounds how long it waits for a response body after the request has been sent, which must accommodate genuinely slow generation work.

The web framework's multipart handling is configured with a maximum file size and a maximum total request size, both defaulting to twenty megabytes and both overridable by environment variable. These framework-level limits are enforced before the request ever reaches application code, so a submission larger than the configured ceiling is rejected during parsing. Any additional ceiling applied inside a service method is a second, independent limit, and the two are not automatically kept in agreement with one another.

The gateway reads the front-end origin from configuration so that cross-origin requests can be permitted from exactly that host, and it toggles the secure attribute on authentication cookies through a separate environment variable so that local development over plain HTTP still works while deployments enforce transport security. It also enables framework handling of forwarded headers, which is what allows the true client address to be recovered when the application sits behind a reverse proxy.

Storage is selected through a provider property that defaults to the local filesystem, paired with a location property giving the directory where uploaded files are written. Routing every storage call through an interface with the implementation chosen by configuration means that swapping the local directory for an object store later is a matter of adding an implementation and changing one property, without touching the service that calls it.

Each feature area of the gateway is split into an api package holding the interface and the transfer objects that other features are allowed to depend on, and an internal package holding the controller, the persistence entity, the repository, the mapper and the implementation. Cross-feature references are therefore expected to go through the published interface rather than reaching into another feature's entities, which keeps the persistence model of one area from becoming part of the contract of another.

The interface is planned as seven screens: a centred login card, a registration flow with a password strength indicator, an empty chat state, an active conversation view supporting markdown rendering and file attachments, a history table of past conversations, a profile dashboard, and a settings screen for managing uploaded files. A fixed sidebar carries the primary navigation and a fixed header carries branding and the account menu.

An embedding maps a piece of text to a fixed-length list of numbers positioned so that texts with similar meaning land near one another. The mapping is learned rather than designed, which is why two passages sharing no vocabulary can still be neighbours while two passages sharing most of their words can be far apart. Retrieval systems exploit this by embedding stored passages once ahead of time and embedding each incoming question at request time, then returning whichever stored vectors sit closest to the question vector.

Cosine similarity compares the angle between two vectors while ignoring their lengths, which is what makes it the usual choice for comparing text representations of different sizes. When every vector has already been scaled to unit length, the cosine reduces to a plain dot product and the ranking it produces is identical to the ranking produced by Euclidean distance, so the choice between those metrics stops mattering. Skipping the scaling step, however, lets long passages dominate purely because they carry larger magnitudes.

Scaling each vector to unit length before it is stored is cheap insurance. It makes the distance operator chosen in the database index consistent with the similarity the model was trained to produce, it lets the engine substitute the faster dot product, and it keeps scores in a bounded and interpretable range. The step must be applied identically when storing and when querying; normalizing only one side produces scores that still rank plausibly but no longer mean what the threshold logic assumes they mean.

Several widely used retrieval models were trained with short instruction strings glued to the front of their inputs, using one marker for questions and a different marker for stored passages. The model learned to place the two into slightly different regions, which is what lets a short question match a long answer. Omitting these markers is silent: nothing errors, vectors of the correct width still come back, and quality simply drops. It is one of the most common ways a retrieval evaluation is quietly invalidated.

Wider vectors can encode finer distinctions but cost more everywhere downstream: storage grows linearly, index memory grows with it, and every comparison touches more numbers. Doubling the width rarely doubles retrieval quality and often changes it barely at all on narrow domains. Some recent models are trained so that their output can be truncated to a shorter prefix with only a small quality loss, which turns the width into a deployment-time dial rather than a decision frozen at training time.

Sizing the store is arithmetic. A vector of single-precision values occupies four bytes per position, so a 768-wide vector is a little over three kilobytes before any per-row overhead, and a million of them is roughly three gigabytes for the column alone. The approximate index adds its own copy on top, and the original text is stored alongside. Multiplying expected document count by expected chunks per document before choosing a width prevents an unpleasant surprise once real content arrives.

The inverted-file approach clusters vectors and scans only the closest clusters, is fast to build, uses little memory, and needs representative data present before the clusters are computed. The graph-based approach links each vector to its neighbours and walks the graph at query time, giving better recall at the same speed, at the cost of a much slower build and considerably more memory. For collections in the low hundreds of thousands the graph approach is usually worth the build time; below a few thousand vectors an exact scan beats both.

Recall at k asks whether the correct passage appeared anywhere in the top k results, which is the question that matters when the results are all handed to a language model anyway. Reciprocal rank instead rewards putting the correct passage first, averaging the inverse of its position across the evaluation set. Reporting both is informative: a system with strong recall but weak reciprocal rank is finding the right material and ordering it badly, which is a reranking problem rather than a retrieval problem.

A two-stage arrangement uses a fast model to retrieve a few dozen candidates and a slower, more accurate model to reorder them. The second stage reads the question and the candidate together rather than encoding them separately, which lets it judge relevance far more precisely but makes it impossible to precompute, so its cost scales with the number of candidates examined at query time. It is the usual first remedy when the right passage is being retrieved but buried below weaker matches.

Dense retrieval handles paraphrase well and exact identifiers badly. A question containing a part number, an error code or an unusual proper noun is often served better by classical keyword scoring, which matches the literal token. Combining the two rankings, either by weighted score fusion or by blending positions, reliably beats either alone on mixed workloads. The cost is a second index to build, keep synchronised and tune, which is why it is usually deferred until the dense-only baseline is measured.

Encoding texts one at a time wastes most of the available compute, because the fixed overhead of a forward pass dominates and the hardware sits idle between calls. Grouping inputs into batches raises throughput dramatically until memory becomes the constraint, at which point larger batches simply fail. The useful operating point is usually found empirically. Batching also interacts with padding: mixing very short and very long inputs in one batch pads everything to the longest, wasting the work it was meant to save.

Every encoder has a maximum input length measured in tokens, and text beyond that limit is discarded rather than summarised. Many established models stop at 512 tokens, roughly 350 to 400 English words, while newer ones accept several thousand. Truncation is usually silent, so a system that feeds oversized passages loses their endings without any warning appearing in the logs. Counting tokens rather than characters before encoding is the only reliable way to know whether content is being dropped.

Loading model weights into memory takes seconds, and downloading them the first time takes considerably longer. A service that loads on first request therefore makes some unlucky user absorb that delay, and one that loads per request is unusable. Loading once during startup and pushing a throwaway input through the model to trigger lazy initialisation moves the entire cost before the service reports itself ready. The trade is a slower start, which matters for autoscaling and for health-check timeouts.

Running several worker processes multiplies memory consumption, because each process loads its own independent copy of the weights. On a machine with limited accelerator memory this is the difference between working and failing to start. Since encoding is already compute-bound and releases no useful concurrency between requests, adding workers rarely helps throughput anyway; batching inside one worker is the better lever, and a single process with a queue in front of it is usually the right shape.

Storing vector components at reduced precision cuts memory substantially with modest quality loss. Halving the precision of each value halves the storage, and aggressive schemes that keep only the sign of each component shrink the store by a factor of thirty-two while retaining a surprising amount of ranking quality, particularly when used as a first pass whose survivors are rescored at full precision. Whether the technique is available depends on the database engine as much as on the model.

Public leaderboards aggregate dozens of tasks into a single average, which is useful for narrowing a shortlist and misleading as a final answer. The aggregate is dominated by task families that may have nothing to do with the intended workload, and models are sometimes tuned against the very benchmarks used to rank them. The average is best read as a filter that removes clearly weak candidates, after which the shortlist should be measured on data drawn from the actual domain.

A model trained only on English will still return vectors for text in other languages, and those vectors will be poor without indicating any problem. Multilingual variants place translations of the same sentence near each other, which additionally allows a question in one language to retrieve a passage in another. The capability is not free: at equal size, a multilingual model typically trails a monolingual one on English-only material, because its capacity is spread across every language it covers.

Text recovered from scanned pages carries systematic damage: characters confused for visually similar ones, words fused or split at the wrong places, headers and page numbers interleaved into the body, and column order scrambled. Encoders are reasonably tolerant of scattered character errors because subword tokenisation degrades gracefully, but they cope badly with reordered text, since a passage whose sentences have been shuffled no longer means what it appears to. Detecting low recognition confidence is more valuable than trying to repair the output.

Flattening a table into running text destroys the alignment between a cell and the column heading that gives it meaning. A row rendered as a bare sequence of values loses the association entirely, so a question naming a column and a row cannot match it. Repeating the heading with each value, so that every cell becomes a short self-describing statement, recovers most of the lost retrieval quality at the cost of considerable redundancy in the stored text.

Source code has vocabulary and structure that general text encoders handle only approximately: identifiers run together without spaces, punctuation carries meaning, and two functions may be near-identical in wording while doing entirely different things. Models trained on code learn that identifiers split into meaningful pieces and that structure matters, which improves matching a natural-language description against an implementation. For repositories where the useful signal lives mostly in comments and documentation, a general model is usually sufficient.

A long accepted input length does not oblige a system to use it. Encoding a very long passage into one vector averages away the specific detail that makes any individual sentence findable, so a question about one narrow fact matches weakly against a vector representing many pages. Long context is most useful as headroom that prevents accidental truncation, not as licence to stop dividing documents into focused units.

Hosted encoding is billed per token processed, and the bill has two distinct components: a one-off charge to encode the corpus and a recurring charge for every query thereafter. Corpora are re-encoded more often than expected, because any change of model forces a complete rebuild. Self-hosting converts that variable cost into fixed hardware and operational effort, and the crossover point depends far more on corpus churn than on query volume, since queries are short and passages are not.

Vectors produced by different models, or by different releases of the same model, are not comparable, and mixing them in one collection produces silently wrong rankings rather than an error. Recording the model identity and version alongside every stored vector makes the mismatch detectable and makes a staged migration possible, where the new representation is built beside the old one and traffic is switched only once it has been verified. Without that column the only safe migration is to rebuild everything at once.

Ingestion jobs fail halfway, and when they are retried the safest design makes a repeated run harmless. Deriving a deterministic identifier for each unit of content, and writing with an operation that replaces an existing row rather than adding a second one, means a retry converges on the correct final state regardless of how far the previous attempt progressed. The alternative, deleting everything belonging to the document before reinserting, is simpler to reason about but leaves the document unsearchable while the job runs.

An evaluation set built by copying phrases out of the target passages measures very little, because every candidate system scores nearly perfectly and the differences between them vanish into noise. Questions should be phrased the way a real user would phrase them, using their own vocabulary, and the collection should contain passages that are plausibly but wrongly relevant. Difficulty comes from those near-misses; without them the ranking task is trivial and the resulting numbers cannot distinguish good from mediocre.

def embed_texts(self, texts: list[str], is_query: bool = False) -> list[list[float]]: prefix = self.query_prefix if is_query else self.passage_prefix; prepared = [prefix + t for t in texts]; vectors = self.model.encode(prepared, batch_size=self.batch_size, normalize_embeddings=True, convert_to_numpy=True); return vectors.tolist() # raises ValueError when texts is empty, because the underlying encoder returns an array with no rows and the caller expects one row per input

SELECT c.id, c.content, 1 - (c.embedding <=> $1) AS similarity FROM document_chunks c JOIN documents d ON d.id = c.document_id WHERE d.user_id = $2 ORDER BY c.embedding <=> $1 LIMIT 5; -- the <=> operator is cosine distance, so subtracting from one converts it back to a similarity; the ordering must use the raw distance operator for the index to be usable, and wrapping it in an expression prevents the planner from choosing the index

Subject: decision needed on vector width before Friday. Team, the chunk table still declares the placeholder width and we cannot build the retrieval endpoint until that is settled, because the column type has to match the model output exactly. My recommendation is the 768-wide option: it is what the schema already assumes, it clears the quality bar on our own evaluation set, and it keeps the store to a manageable size. If anyone objects, please reply before Thursday evening so we can close it out.

Einbettungen bilden einen Text auf eine Zahlenfolge fester Länge ab, wobei inhaltlich ähnliche Texte nahe beieinander liegen. Ein rein englischsprachig trainiertes Modell liefert für deutsche Eingaben zwar weiterhin Vektoren, deren Qualität ist jedoch deutlich schlechter, ohne dass ein Fehler gemeldet wird. Mehrsprachige Modelle ordnen Übersetzungen desselben Satzes einander zu und ermöglichen dadurch, dass eine deutsche Frage einen englischen Absatz findet.

El índice aproximado divide los vectores en grupos y consulta únicamente los más cercanos, lo que reduce mucho el número de comparaciones a cambio de una pequeña pérdida de exhaustividad. Debe construirse después de cargar los datos, porque un conjunto vacío produce grupos degenerados. El número de listas se elige normalmente en función de la cantidad de filas almacenadas y conviene revisarlo cuando la colección crece de forma significativa.
